title: Warehouse Platforms Compared
summary: Cloud warehouses split into a few genuinely different compute models — multi-cluster shared-data, serverless, and fixed-cluster MPP. The right one follows from your workload's shape, not from a benchmark headline.

slides.markdown:
[Warehouse Fundamentals](warehouse-fundamentals) covered MPP and storage/compute separation as ideas. Real platforms implement those ideas with real architectural differences — some give you independently scalable clusters sharing one copy of data, some abstract away clusters entirely into a pay-per-query model, some still bundle storage and compute into a fixed cluster you size yourself.

This topic covers those models concretely enough that you can look at a workload — bursty and unpredictable, or steady and predictable — and reason about which compute model actually fits it, instead of picking based on which platform's marketing benchmark looked best.

slides.sectionTitle: The major cloud warehouses' compute models
slides.markdown:
Three broad compute models dominate the current cloud warehouse landscape:

| Model | Representative platforms | Core idea |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-cluster, shared data | Snowflake | Data stored once; multiple independently-sized compute clusters ("virtual warehouses") attach to it, each scaled and billed separately |
| Serverless, no cluster management | BigQuery | No cluster to size at all — the platform allocates compute per query automatically, billed by bytes processed or a flat-rate compute commitment |
| Fixed-cluster MPP | Redshift (provisioned mode) | A traditional MPP cluster you size and provision, closer in spirit to on-premises MPP warehouses, with compute and storage more tightly coupled |

All three genuinely implement the MPP and columnar principles from earlier topics — the difference is entirely in how compute is provisioned, scaled, and billed, not in the underlying query execution ideas.

slides.sectionTitle: Independently scalable clusters on shared storage
slides.markdown:
The multi-cluster, shared-data model stores data once in a shared layer and lets you spin up multiple compute clusters — sized independently, scaled independently, billed independently — all reading and writing the same underlying data.

The direct payoff is workload isolation: a BI team's dashboard-refresh cluster and a data science team's heavy nightly transformation cluster never compete for the same compute resources, because they're literally different clusters, even though they're querying the same tables. Either can be resized (more nodes, bigger nodes) or paused independently without affecting the other.

The cost model that follows is per-cluster, active-time billing — a cluster only costs money while it's running and not suspended, so a workload with predictable idle periods (a dashboard cluster nobody queries overnight) can auto-suspend and stop billing, resuming automatically the moment a new query arrives.

A serverless warehouse removes cluster sizing from the picture entirely — there's no "how many nodes should this cluster have" decision to make at all. You submit a query, the platform allocates whatever compute it decides that query needs behind the scenes, and you're billed based on the query's actual resource consumption (commonly bytes processed) rather than for cluster time.

This is genuinely simpler operationally — no capacity planning, no idle-cluster waste, and it scales naturally from an occasional ad hoc query to a massive batch job without anyone provisioning anything differently. The trade-off is less direct control: you can't tune cluster size or placement for a specific workload's characteristics the way you can with dedicated clusters, and cost predictability shifts from "I know what my cluster costs per hour" to "cost depends on how much data each query actually touches" — which puts a premium on the column-pruning and predicate-pushdown discipline from earlier in this group, since an unnecessarily broad scan translates directly into a bigger bill with no cluster-size ceiling to cap it.

slides.subTitle: Closer to traditional MPP
slides.markdown:
A fixed-cluster model has you provision a cluster of a specific size upfront — a set number of nodes with a set amount of compute and (often) locally-attached storage — and that cluster serves all queries against it until you manually resize it. This is architecturally closer to the traditional, on-premises MPP warehouses that predate cloud elasticity: compute and storage are more tightly coupled, and there's a real provisioning decision to make rather than infinite elastic scaling.

The advantage is predictable, often lower cost for **steady, well-understood workloads** — if you know your query volume and shape well and it doesn't spike unpredictably, a fixed cluster sized correctly can be more cost-efficient than paying the overhead of elastic, per-query billing. The disadvantage is exactly the flip side: a workload that spikes unpredictably either gets throttled by the fixed cluster's capacity or requires the operational overhead of manually resizing ahead of anticipated spikes — something the other two models handle automatically.

Modern versions of fixed-cluster platforms increasingly offer elastic add-ons on top of the base model, blurring this line — but the core distinction (provision-once vs auto-scaling-by-design) still shapes how you plan capacity.

A separate axis from raw compute size is how a platform handles a **burst of simultaneous queries** — a Monday-morning wave of dashboard refreshes hitting all at once, for instance. Multi-cluster and serverless models generally handle this gracefully by design: spin up additional compute (another cluster, or more serverless allocation) to absorb the burst, then scale back down once it passes. A fixed-size cluster has a hard ceiling — once its concurrent-query capacity is saturated, additional queries queue and wait, regardless of how urgent they are.

This matters specifically for workloads with unpredictable concurrency spikes rather than unpredictable data volume — a platform can handle a huge query on a small cluster just fine (given enough time) but choke on a modest query arriving alongside a hundred other modest queries at the same instant, if concurrency isn't handled elastically.

When evaluating a platform for a workload, "how does it behave under concurrent query bursts" is a distinct question from "how does it perform on one large query" — a platform's benchmark numbers often answer only the second.

slides.sectionTitle: Porting a schema across cost models
slides.markdown:
A team migrates from a fixed-cluster platform to a serverless one and ports their schema and queries directly, unchanged — including a handful of `SELECT *` queries and a wide, denormalized table that was fine under fixed-cluster pricing, since that cluster's cost was the same whether a query scanned 10% or 90% of the table.

Under consumption-based serverless pricing, that same wide-table-plus-broad-scan pattern now directly multiplies the bill, because cost tracks bytes actually processed per query rather than cluster-hours. A migration that looked like a clean lift-and-shift produces a cost surprise entirely because the *pricing model* changed underneath queries that were never designed with bytes-scanned cost in mind.

The fix is treating a platform migration as an opportunity (really a requirement) to revisit query and schema design against the new cost model — applying column pruning discipline, checking for unnecessary `SELECT *`, and reconsidering whether a wide table should be restructured — rather than assuming a query that was cost-neutral on one platform stays cost-neutral on another with a fundamentally different pricing mechanism.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing by workload shape, not benchmarks
slides.markdown:
Public benchmark comparisons between platforms are almost always run on a specific, standardized query set at a specific data size — useful as one data point, but a poor substitute for reasoning about your own workload's actual shape:

- **Steady, predictable, high-utilization** workload → a fixed-cluster model can be genuinely cost-efficient, since you're not paying elastic-scaling overhead for a workload that doesn't need it.
- **Bursty, unpredictable, or infrequent** workload → serverless or multi-cluster models avoid paying for idle capacity and absorb spikes without manual intervention.
- **Multiple teams with genuinely different, competing usage patterns** → multi-cluster shared-data lets each team's compute scale and cost independently against the same underlying data.

The practical move: profile your *own* actual query patterns — volume, concurrency, predictability, team isolation needs — before comparing platforms, and treat a benchmark's headline number as context, not as the decision.

Put this on a concrete scenario: a company has a BI team running frequent, small dashboard queries all day, and a data science team running a few enormous training-data extraction jobs overnight, with no other teams involved.

A fixed-cluster model sized for the BI team's steady load would either be too small for the nightly extraction (causing it to queue or run painfully slowly) or oversized and wastefully idle most of the day if sized for the extraction job instead — there's no single fixed size that serves both well. A multi-cluster shared-data model solves this cleanly: a small, always-on cluster for BI (cheap, since it's small and constantly utilized) and a large cluster that spins up only for the nightly extraction and suspends afterward (paying for size only during the hours it's actually needed) — both querying the same underlying tables with zero contention between them.

This is exactly the kind of reasoning — matching each distinct workload to the compute shape it actually needs, rather than picking one model for the whole organization — that the previous slide's "profile before choosing" advice looks like in practice.

Compute model is one axis of warehouse choice; how data is physically organized within a table is an orthogonal one that matters regardless of which platform you pick. The next topic, Partitioning & Clustering for Query Performance, covers exactly that — the physical-layout techniques that determine how much of a table any given query actually has to scan, which directly interacts with every cost model covered here: less scanned data means a cheaper serverless query, less compute-time on a fixed cluster, and faster results everywhere.

Carry forward the throughline: the compute model changes how you pay and how elastically you scale, but it doesn't change the underlying MPP-and-columnar mechanics from earlier in this group — those apply regardless of which platform, or which pricing model, sits on top of them.
